topics.title: The statistical investigation process
points: The investigation cycle: pose a question, collect data, analyse the data, interpret and communicate the results.
A population is the whole group of interest; a sample is the part that is measured.
Random sampling reduces bias; a biased sample does not represent the population.
Observational studies record what happens; experiments change one variable and observe the effect.
Conclusions should answer the question, use the evidence and state limitations.
topics.explain: Design a short investigation into whether students at your school who play sport sleep more. Describe each stage of the cycle.

p: This is the first lesson in General Mathematics, and you need nothing before it.

The big idea: statistics is about answering questions with data. The calculations in the following lessons only matter because they help answer a question. This lesson sets out the process every data analysis follows, so that you always know why you are calculating something.

1. Pose a question that data can answer. “Do Year 11 students spend more time on homework than Year 9 students?” is specific and measurable; “Is homework good?” is not. 2. Plan and collect data: decide who to ask, which variables to record and how. 3. Analyse: organise, display and summarise the data. 4. Interpret and communicate: answer the question in context, using the evidence, and note any limitations.
The cycle often repeats: the results may suggest a new or sharper question.
check: Rewrite “Is social media bad?” as a statistical question.
For example: “Do students who spend more than 3 hours a day on social media have lower average test scores than those who spend less?”

fig.cap: The statistical investigation cycle. Results often lead to a new, sharper question.

p: The population is everyone or everything the question is about, such as all Year 11 students in Victoria. A census measures the whole population; it is complete but usually too costly. A sample measures part of it, and the results are used to make conclusions about the population.

A good sample is representative. Random sampling, where every member has an equal chance of selection, is the main protection against bias. A sample can be biased if it is self-selected (only people who choose to answer an online poll), convenient (only your own friends) or drawn from the wrong group. Larger samples give more reliable estimates, but a large biased sample is still biased.

fig.cap: A random sample (filled) drawn from a population. Every member had an equal chance of being chosen.

p: Surveys ask questions; good questions are clear, neutral and have answer options that cover all cases. “Don’t you agree that school starts too early?” is a leading question. Observations record behaviour directly. Measurements record quantities such as heights or times. Secondary data, collected by someone else such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics, can answer questions at a scale you could not reach yourself.

An observational study records variables without changing anything. An experiment deliberately changes the explanatory variable, ideally assigning subjects at random to groups, and measures the response. Only a well-designed experiment can provide strong evidence of cause and effect.

Answer the original question directly, using statistics as evidence: “The median homework time for Year 11 (12 hours per week) was higher than for Year 9 (7 hours per week), so the data suggest Year 11 students spend more time on homework.” Then note limitations: sample size, how the sample was chosen, whether the data were self-reported, and whether the result can be generalised.
Avoid claiming more than the data show. A difference in a small sample may be due to chance; an association in an observational study does not prove causation.

Questions that cannot be answered with data. Samples chosen for convenience then treated as representative. Leading survey questions. Conclusions that ignore the original question or that claim causation from an observational study.

qs.q: Which sampling method is most likely to give a representative sample?
o: An online poll anyone can answer
Choosing names at random from the full school list
Asking the first 20 students to arrive
qs.e: Random selection from the whole population reduces bias.

qs.q: An investigation records students’ screen time and sleep without changing anything. This is…
List the four stages of the statistical investigation cycle.
qs.a: Pose a question; collect data; analyse the data; interpret and communicate the results.

qs.q: What is wrong with the survey question “How much do you love our new canteen menu?”
qs.a: It is a leading question: it assumes the respondent loves the menu and pushes towards a positive answer.

qs.q: Measuring every member of a population is called a…
Which is a statistical question?
o: How many hours per week do Year 11 students at this school spend on homework?
How many hours did I sleep last night?
qs.e: It anticipates variation and can be answered with data.

qs.q: 50 randomly chosen Year 12 students in Victoria are surveyed about their sleep. Identify the population and the sample.
qs.a: Population: all Year 12 students in Victoria. Sample: the 50 students surveyed.

qs.q: A radio station asks listeners to phone in their opinion. The main problem with this sample is that it is…
Why can an observational study not show that one variable causes another?
qs.a: Other variables may be confounded with the explanatory variable, so the effect cannot be separated. Only a randomised experiment controls for this.

qs.q: In an experiment, subjects are allocated to groups at random so that…
o: the groups are similar apart from the treatment

topics.title: Univariate data
points: Categorical data: nominal (no order) or ordinal (ordered). Numerical data: discrete (counted) or continuous (measured).
Centre: mean \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum x}{n}\) (affected by outliers) and median (resistant). Spread: range, \(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\), standard deviation \(s\).
Outliers lie below \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) or above \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\).
Shape: symmetric, positively skewed (tail to the right), negatively skewed (tail to the left).
Displays: bar charts for categorical data; histograms, dot plots, stem plots and boxplots for numerical data.
topics.explain: Explain why the median is a better measure of centre than the mean for house prices.

qs.q: Postcode is which type of data?
A distribution with a long tail to the right is…
Find the mean and median of \(2, 4, 6, 8, 10\).
Find the five-number summary of 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12.
s: There are 7 values, so the median is the 4th: 7.
Lower half 2, 4, 5: Q₁ = 4. Upper half 8, 10, 12: Q₃ = 10.

qs.q: For the data 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, find the IQR and the outlier fences. Are there any outliers?
s: Every value lies between −5 and 19, so there are no outliers.

qs.q: For a positively skewed distribution, the mean is usually…
qs.e: The long right tail pulls the mean up.

qs.q: A postcode is which type of variable?
qs.e: The digits are labels, not quantities.

qs.q: Find the mean, median and mode of 3, 5, 8, 12, 12.
Which statistic is least affected by an outlier?
Find the mean of these scores: [[a]], [[b]], [[c]], [[d]], [[f]].

p: Before this lesson you should have read the lesson on the statistical investigation process, and be able to calculate a mean and a median.

The big idea: a single variable, such as the heights of a class or the prices of houses, is summarised by its shape, centre and spread. Choosing the right display and the right statistics, and then describing what they show in context, is the core skill of the data analysis area of study.

Before choosing a display or a statistic, classify the variable. Categorical variables put individuals into groups: nominal if the groups have no order (eye colour), ordinal if they do (satisfaction rating). Numerical variables are counts or measurements: discrete if only separate values are possible (number of siblings), continuous if any value in a range is possible (height). A variable recorded with digits is not always numerical: postcodes and jersey numbers are nominal.

Median: the middle value of the ordered data, at position \(\dfrac{n + 1}{2}\). Quartiles split the data into four equal parts; \(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\) is the spread of the middle 50%. Range is the maximum minus the minimum. The standard deviation measures the typical distance of values from the mean.

Use the median and IQR when the distribution is skewed or has outliers, because they are not affected by extreme values. Use the mean and standard deviation when the distribution is roughly symmetric with no outliers.
check: Find the median of 3, 8, 9, 12.
The middle two values are 8 and 9, so the median is 8.5.

p: \(n = 9\), so the median is the 5th value, 8. Lower half 3, 5, 6, 7 gives \(Q_1 = 5.5\); upper half 9, 10, 12, 30 gives \(Q_3 = 11\). \(\text{IQR} = 5.5\). Upper fence \(= 11 + 1.5 \times 5.5 = 19.25\), so 30 is an outlier. Lower fence \(= 5.5 - 8.25 = -2.75\), so there are no low outliers. The mean is 10, pulled above the median by the outlier.

A full description covers shape (symmetric, positively or negatively skewed, number of modes), centre (median or mean), spread (IQR, range or standard deviation) and outliers, always with values and in context. In a boxplot the whisker ends at the last data value inside the fence, and outliers are drawn as separate points.

To compare groups with parallel boxplots, compare medians and IQRs and quote them: “The median for group A (24) is higher than for group B (18), and its IQR is smaller (5 compared with 9), so A’s values are higher and more consistent.”

Categorical data: a bar chart for one variable, a segmented (stacked) percentage bar chart for comparing groups. Small sets of numerical data: a dot plot or stem plot, which show every value. Larger sets of numerical data: a histogram, which groups values into intervals. Comparing a numerical variable across groups: parallel boxplots or a back-to-back stem plot.

A histogram has no gaps between columns, because the intervals are continuous; a bar chart has gaps, because categories are separate. When data cover several orders of magnitude, such as city populations, a log scale on the horizontal axis can make the distribution readable.
check: Which display suits the favourite sport of 30 students?
A bar chart (or a segmented bar chart): the variable is categorical.

fig.cap: A histogram of 40 test scores: columns touch because the intervals are continuous. This one is slightly negatively skewed.

notes.h: Worked example: mean and standard deviation
p: Data: 4, 7, 7, 8, 9. Mean \(= \dfrac{35}{5} = 7\). Deviations from the mean: \(-3, 0, 0, 1, 2\). Squared: 9, 0, 0, 1, 4, which total 14. Standard deviation \(s = \sqrt{\dfrac{14}{5 - 1}} = \sqrt{3.5} \approx 1.87\).
In practice technology calculates s, but knowing what it measures (the typical distance of values from the mean) lets you interpret it. A larger standard deviation means more spread.
check: An outlier is removed from a data set. Which changes more, the mean or the median?
The mean, because it uses the value of every data point; the median depends only on the middle position.

p: Parallel boxplots show test results for two classes. Class A: median 72, IQR 10, no outliers, roughly symmetric. Class B: median 65, IQR 18, one low outlier at 20, negatively skewed.

Model answer: “The median score for Class A (72) is higher than for Class B (65), so Class A students typically scored higher. The IQR for Class A (10) is smaller than for Class B (18), so Class A’s results are more consistent. Class A’s distribution is approximately symmetric, while Class B’s is negatively skewed with a low outlier at 20.” Each sentence names both groups, quotes both values and says what they mean.

fig.cap: Parallel boxplots. Class A has a higher median (72 vs 65) and smaller IQR (10 vs 18); Class B has a low outlier at 20.

p: Finding the median of unordered data. Describing skew the wrong way: the name follows the tail. Calling a value an outlier without calculating the fence. Quoting the mean for strongly skewed data.

topics.title: Investigating relationships
points: Explanatory variable on the \(x\)-axis, response variable on the \(y\)-axis.
Describe a scatterplot by direction (positive or negative), form (linear or non-linear) and strength (weak, moderate, strong).
Pearson’s correlation coefficient: \(-1 \le r \le 1\). It only measures linear relationships.
Correlation does not mean causation: a third variable may explain both.
Two-way tables and segmented bar charts compare two categorical variables.
topics.explain: Explain why ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated but one does not cause the other.

qs.q: \(r = -0.85\) describes a…
Height and shoe size: which is explanatory if you want to predict shoe size?
In “Does temperature affect ice-cream sales?”, the explanatory variable is…
Describe the association shown by \(r = 0.45\).
qs.a: A moderate, positive, linear association (assuming the scatterplot is linear with no outliers).

qs.q: Which value of \(r\) shows the strongest linear association?
qs.e: Strength depends on the size of r, not its sign.

qs.q: A line of good fit is score = 40 + 5 × hours. Predict the score for 7 hours of study and interpret the slope.
qs.a: 75; the score increases by 5 marks, on average, for each extra hour of study
s: The slope 5 is the average increase in score for each additional hour.

qs.q: 30 of 50 boys and 20 of 50 girls prefer online games. Is preference associated with gender?
qs.a: Yes: 60% of boys compared with 40% of girls
s: The percentages differ noticeably, so there is an association.

qs.q: A study finds people who drink more coffee earn more. Which conclusion is justified?
o: Coffee drinking and income are associated
Earning more makes people drink coffee
qs.e: Observational data show association, not causation.

qs.q: Find the equation of the line through (2, 10) and (6, 22).
A prediction made well outside the range of the data is…
The least squares line is \(\text{height} = [[a]] + [[b]] \times \text{age}\). Predict the height (cm) at age [[x]].

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with univariate data and with straight-line graphs.

The big idea: often we want to know whether two variables are related, such as study time and results, or age and preferred music. This lesson shows how to display a relationship, describe it in words, and summarise it with a line, while being careful not to claim that one variable causes the other.

The explanatory variable is the one used to explain or predict; the response variable is the one being explained. In “does study time affect test score?”, study time is explanatory. Put the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis.

For two numerical variables, describe the scatterplot in four parts: direction, form, strength and outliers. As a guide to strength: \(|r|\) from 0.75 to 1 is strong, 0.5 to 0.74 moderate, 0.25 to 0.49 weak, below 0.25 no association. \(r\) is only meaningful for linear associations with no outliers.
Model sentence: “There is a strong, positive, linear association between hours studied and test score, with no apparent outliers. Students who study for longer tend to score higher.”

A line fitted by eye, or by least squares with technology, summarises a linear association. Interpret the slope as the change in the response variable for each one-unit increase in the explanatory variable, and the intercept as the predicted response when the explanatory variable is zero (if that makes sense in context).
Example: \(\text{score} = 42 + 5.5 \times \text{hours}\). On average, the score increases by 5.5 marks for each extra hour of study. For 6 hours: \(42 + 33 = 75\) marks.

For two categorical variables use a two-way frequency table and convert to percentages, with the explanatory variable defining the columns and each column adding to 100%. An association exists if the percentages differ noticeably across the columns.
Example: 60% of Year 11 students and 35% of Year 12 students play a sport. Since the percentages differ, participation in sport is associated with year level. Quote the percentages as evidence.

A strong association does not show that one variable causes the other. The explanation could be a common response to a third variable (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature), confounding (several possible causes mixed together) or coincidence.
check: Ice-cream sales and sunburn cases rise together. Suggest a reason that does not involve one causing the other.
Both are responses to a third variable: hot, sunny weather.

p: A scatterplot of hours of sleep (explanatory) against reaction time in milliseconds (response) for 20 students shows points falling from left to right in a roughly straight band, with no outliers; \(r = -0.82\).

Description: “There is a strong, negative, linear association between hours of sleep and reaction time, with no outliers. Students who sleep more tend to have shorter reaction times.” Then a caution: this is an observational study, so it does not show that extra sleep causes faster reactions.
check: What four features should a description of a scatterplot include?
Direction, form, strength and any outliers, stated in context.

fig.cap: Hours of sleep and reaction time: a strong, negative, linear association with no outliers (r ≈ −0.82).

p: Draw a line through the middle of the points so that roughly equal numbers lie above and below it. Choose two points on the line far apart, for example \((2, 50)\) and \((10, 90)\). Slope \(= \dfrac{90 - 50}{10 - 2} = 5\). Intercept: \(50 = a + 5 \times 2\), so \(a = 40\). Equation: \(\text{score} = 40 + 5 \times \text{hours}\).
Use it to predict within the range of the data, and be cautious outside it. The least squares line from technology does the same job more objectively; it is developed in Units 3 and 4.
check: A line passes through (0, 12) and (4, 20). What is its equation?

p: 200 students are surveyed. Of 100 Year 11 students, 60 play sport; of 100 Year 12 students, 35 play sport. As column percentages: Year 11, 60% play and 40% do not; Year 12, 35% play and 65% do not.

Because the percentage who play sport is noticeably different between the year levels (60% and 35%), there is an association between year level and sport participation. Always compare percentages, not counts, because group sizes are often unequal.

fig.cap: Column percentages: 60% of Year 11 and 35% of Year 12 students play sport, so participation is associated with year level.
head: Plays sport?
Year 11
Year 12

p: Reversing the variables. Using causal language (“causes”, “leads to”) from observational data. Comparing counts instead of percentages in a two-way table. Describing strength without direction and form.

topics.title: Percentages, interest and recursion
points: Percentage change \(= \dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{original}} \times 100\%\). GST: price \(\times 1.1\); GST in a total \(= \dfrac{\text{total}}{11}\).
Simple interest: \(I = \dfrac{PrT}{100}\); total value \(A = P + I\).
Compound interest: \(A = P\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^n\).
Linear recurrence \(u_{n+1} = u_n + d\) (simple interest, flat-rate depreciation). Geometric recurrence \(u_{n+1} = Ru_n\) (compound growth or decay).
Inflation reduces purchasing power; compare costs in today’s dollars.
topics.explain: Explain why compound interest grows faster than simple interest over time.

qs.q: Find the simple interest on $5 000 at 4% p.a. for 3 years.
$1 000 is invested at 5% p.a. compounding annually. Find its value after 2 years.
A $80 item rises to $92. Find the percentage increase.
Find the simple interest on $4000 at 3.5% per annum for 3 years.
$4000 is invested at 3.5% per annum compounding annually. Find its value after 3 years.

o: linear decay, such as flat-rate depreciation

qs.q: An item costs $85. Find its price after a 20% discount.
A price rises from $50 to $62. Find the percentage increase.
Find the simple interest earned on $[[=P|,0]] at [[r]]% per annum for [[t]] years.
$[[=P|,0]] is invested at [[r]]% per annum compounding monthly. Find its value after [[t]] years, to the nearest cent.
A price rises from $[[a]] to $[[b]]. Find the percentage increase, to 1 decimal place.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with percentages and with substituting into formulas.

The big idea: money grows or shrinks in one of two ways. Either the same amount is added or taken each period (linear), or the same percentage is (geometric). Recurrence relations describe both, step by step, and the same idea runs right through the financial mathematics in Units 3 and 4.
To increase by \(r\%\), multiply by \(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\); to decrease, multiply by \(1 - \dfrac{r}{100}\). To undo a percentage change, divide by the same multiplier.
Example: a price including 10% GST is $165. The price before GST is \(165 \div 1.1 = \$150\), and the GST is $15. Taking 10% off $165 gives the wrong answer.

Simple interest is earned on the original principal only, so the balance grows by the same amount each period (linear growth). Compound interest is earned on the principal and on earlier interest, so the balance grows by the same percentage each period (geometric growth) and the gap widens over time.

Example: $5000 at 6% per annum for 4 years. Simple: \(I = \dfrac{5000 \times 6 \times 4}{100} = \$1200\), total $6200. Compound annually: \(A = 5000 \times 1.06^4 = \$6312.38\). Compounding monthly: \(A = 5000 \times 1.005^{48} = \$6352.45\).

A recurrence relation gives a starting value and a rule for getting each term from the one before. \(u_0 = 5000,\ u_{n+1} = u_n + 300\) models simple interest (add the same amount). \(u_0 = 5000,\ u_{n+1} = 1.06u_n\) models compound interest (multiply by the same factor). A first-order linear recurrence \(u_{n+1} = Ru_n + d\) combines both, for example a savings account with regular deposits.
Generate terms one at a time and write each one down: \(u_1 = 1.06 \times 5000 = 5300\), \(u_2 = 1.06 \times 5300 = 5618\).
check: Generate the first three terms of \(u_0 = 10,\ u_{n+1} = 3u_n - 4\).

p: Arithmetic: common difference \(d\), with \(u_n = u_0 + nd\). Geometric: common ratio \(r\), with \(u_n = u_0 r^n\). If the first term is called \(u_1\), the rules use \(n - 1\) in place of \(n\). Check which the question uses.

Compare cash, credit and buy-now-pay-later by total cost. Example: a $1200 laptop bought with a $200 deposit and 24 monthly payments of $50 costs \(200 + 1200 = \$1400\); the extra $200 is interest on the $1000 borrowed. Flat rate over 2 years \(= \dfrac{200}{1000 \times 2} \times 100 = 10\%\) per annum.

$1000 earns 10% per annum. Simple interest adds $100 each year: $1100, $1200, $1300. Compound interest adds 10% of the current balance: $1100, $1210, $1331. On a graph, simple interest gives points on a straight line; compound interest gives points on an upward curve that pulls further ahead each year.
The longer the term and the higher the rate, the bigger the difference. This is why compounding is described as earning “interest on interest”.
check: $2000 is invested at 5% per annum. What is the balance after 2 years with simple interest, and with annual compounding?

fig.cap: $1000 at 10% per annum: simple interest grows by $100 a year (straight line); compound interest grows by 10% a year and pulls ahead.

p: A student has $1000 in an account paying 0.5% interest per month and deposits $100 at the end of each month. Recurrence relation: \(u_0 = 1000,\ u_{n+1} = 1.005u_n + 100\).

\(u_1 = 1.005 \times 1000 + 100 = 1105\). \(u_2 = 1.005 \times 1105 + 100 = 1210.53\) (to the nearest cent). \(u_3 = 1.005 \times 1210.525 + 100 = 1316.58\). Keep full accuracy in the calculator between steps.
check: Write a recurrence relation for $500 invested at 2% per year with $50 added each year.

p: Inflation is the general rise in prices. With 3% inflation per year, an item costing $100 today will cost about \(100 \times 1.03^5 = \$115.93\) in five years. If a wage rises by only 2% per year over the same period, the wage buys less each year: its purchasing power falls.
To compare amounts from different years fairly, convert them to the same year’s dollars by applying the inflation rate.

Using the annual rate without dividing by the number of compounding periods. Subtracting a percentage from the final price to undo an increase. Mixing up \(u_0\) and \(u_1\). Rounding before the final step.

topics.title: Matrices
points: Order = rows \(\times\) columns. Add or subtract matrices only of the same order.
\(AB\) exists if the number of columns of \(A\) equals the number of rows of \(B\): \((m \times n)(n \times p)\) gives an \(m \times p\) matrix.
Matrix multiplication is not usually commutative: \(AB \neq BA\).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\): \(\det A = ad - bc\) and \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}\), which exists only if \(\det A \neq 0\).
Matrices store data in tables and can solve simultaneous equations.
topics.explain: Explain why a \(2 \times 3\) matrix cannot be multiplied by another \(2 \times 3\) matrix.

qs.q: \(A\) is \(2 \times 3\) and \(B\) is \(3 \times 4\). The order of \(AB\) is…
Find \(\det\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
The order of \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\) is…
Find \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
Find \(3\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
A \(2 \times 3\) matrix multiplied by a \(3 \times 1\) matrix gives a matrix of order…
qs.e: The inner numbers match; the outer numbers give the order.

qs.q: Find the determinant and inverse of \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).
s: Swap the leading diagonal, negate the other diagonal.

qs.q: For two square matrices A and B, AB and BA are…
Use a matrix inverse to solve \(2x + y = 5\) and \(x + y = 3\).
A customer buys 2 pies and 3 drinks. Pies cost $4 and drinks $5. Write this as a matrix product and find the total.
s: Quantities as a row matrix, prices as a column matrix.

qs.q: Find the determinant of \(\begin{bmatrix} [[a]] & [[b]] \\ [[c]] & [[d]] \end{bmatrix}\).

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with basic arithmetic and with solving simultaneous equations.

The big idea: a matrix is a table of numbers that can be calculated with. Matrices store data neatly, combine quantities with prices in one step, and solve systems of equations. In Units 3 and 4 they model networks and populations that change over time.

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. Its order is rows by columns, and element \(a_{ij}\) is in row \(i\) and column \(j\). Row matrices have one row, column matrices one column, and square matrices the same number of each. The identity matrix \(I\) has ones on the leading diagonal and zeros elsewhere, and \(AI = IA = A\).

Add, subtract and multiply by a number (scalar) element by element. To multiply two matrices, each element of the product is a row of the first multiplied by a column of the second, added up. An \(m \times n\) matrix times an \(n \times p\) matrix gives an \(m \times p\) matrix.

Example: \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 4 + 1 \times 5 \\ 0 \times 4 + 3 \times 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix}\).

Store quantities in one matrix and prices in another, and the product gives totals. Example: a shop sells 3 pies and 2 drinks on Monday and 5 pies and 4 drinks on Tuesday; pies cost $6 and drinks $3. \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 24 \\ 42 \end{bmatrix}\): takings of $24 and $42. The labels on the columns of the first matrix must match the labels on the rows of the second.

fig.cap: Quantities times prices: the labels on the columns of the first matrix match the labels on the rows of the second.

p: The inverse \(A^{-1}\) satisfies \(AA^{-1} = I\). It exists only for square matrices with a non-zero determinant. For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, swap the leading diagonal, change the signs of the other diagonal and divide by the determinant.
Example: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). \(\det A = 6 - 5 = 1\), so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
check: Find the determinant of \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(4 \times 2 - 2 \times 3 = 2\).

p: Write the system as \(AX = B\), then \(X = A^{-1}B\). Example: \(3x + y = 7\) and \(5x + 2y = 12\). \(X = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(x = 2\), \(y = 1\). If the determinant is zero there is no unique solution.

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). Row 1 times column 1: \(1 \times 0 + 2 \times 5 = 10\). Row 1 times column 2: \(1 \times 1 + 2 \times 2 = 5\). Row 2 times column 1: \(3 \times 0 + 4 \times 5 = 20\). Row 2 times column 2: \(3 \times 1 + 4 \times 2 = 11\). Result: \(\begin{bmatrix} 10 & 5 \\ 20 & 11 \end{bmatrix}\).

In the other order, \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 11 & 18 \end{bmatrix}\), a different answer. The order of multiplication matters.
check: Find \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix}\).

p: Zero matrix: every element 0. Identity matrix \(I\): ones on the leading diagonal, zeros elsewhere. Diagonal matrix: non-zero elements only on the leading diagonal. Symmetric matrix: equal to its transpose, so \(a_{ij} = a_{ji}\). Triangular matrix: all elements above (or below) the leading diagonal are zero. Binary matrix: only 0s and 1s.
The transpose \(A^T\) swaps rows and columns: the first row becomes the first column. If \(A\) is \(2 \times 3\), \(A^T\) is \(3 \times 2\).
check: What is the order of \(A^T\) if \(A\) is a \(3 \times 1\) matrix?

p: Multiplying in the wrong order: \(A^{-1}B\) is not \(BA^{-1}\). Multiplying matrices element by element. Attempting a product whose orders do not match. Forgetting to divide by the determinant.

topics.title: Graphs and networks
points: A graph has vertices joined by edges; the degree of a vertex is the number of edges at it.
Euler trail (every edge once): exists if exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree. Euler circuit (returns to start): every degree is even.
Hamiltonian path: visits every vertex once. Hamiltonian cycle: also returns to the start.
Connected planar graphs satisfy Euler’s formula \(v - e + f = 2\).
Trees, spanning trees and shortest paths solve real problems such as routes and cabling.

A connected planar graph has [[v]] vertices and [[e]] edges. How many faces does it have?

p: You can start this lesson with no prerequisites beyond basic arithmetic.

The big idea: a network reduces a real situation (roads, friendships, pipes, a project) to dots and lines, so that questions such as “what is the shortest route?” or “can every street be travelled once?” can be answered systematically. The vocabulary is precise, so learn it carefully.

A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges. A loop joins a vertex to itself and adds 2 to its degree. The sum of all degrees is twice the number of edges. A connected graph has a path between every pair of vertices. A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph. A planar graph can be drawn with no edges crossing; its regions, including the outside one, are faces.

A walk is any sequence of connected edges. A trail is a walk with no repeated edge. A path is a walk with no repeated vertex. A circuit is a trail that starts and ends at the same vertex. A cycle is a path that returns to its start.
Eulerian questions are about edges (a postie walking every street); Hamiltonian questions are about vertices (a courier visiting every town).

Count the degree of every vertex. All even: an Eulerian circuit exists, starting anywhere. Exactly two odd: an Eulerian trail exists, starting at one odd vertex and ending at the other. Any other number of odd vertices: neither exists.

Example: degrees 2, 3, 3, 4, 4. Two odd vertices, so there is an Eulerian trail but no Eulerian circuit. To make a circuit possible, add an edge joining the two odd vertices. There is no quick test for Hamiltonian paths; find one by trial.
check: A connected graph has vertex degrees 2, 2, 4, 3, 3. Does it have an Eulerian circuit, an Eulerian trail, or neither?
An Eulerian trail (exactly two odd vertices), but not a circuit.

fig.cap: Degrees A 2, B 3, C 4, D 3, E 2. Exactly two odd vertices (B and D), so an Eulerian trail exists from B to D, but no circuit.

p: Example: a connected planar graph has 6 vertices and 9 edges. \(f = 2 - v + e = 2 - 6 + 9 = 5\) faces. To check a claim, substitute: if the numbers do not satisfy the formula, the graph is not a connected planar graph.

A tree is a connected graph with no cycles; a tree with \(n\) vertices has \(n - 1\) edges. A spanning tree connects all the vertices of a graph. A minimum spanning tree has the smallest total weight and gives the cheapest way to connect every location, such as laying cable. Prim’s algorithm: start at any vertex, repeatedly add the smallest-weight edge that connects a new vertex, and stop when every vertex is included.
A shortest path is the route of least total weight between two given vertices. It need not use every vertex.

An adjacency matrix records how many edges join each pair of vertices. Rows and columns are labelled with the vertices in the same order. For an undirected graph the matrix is symmetric. A loop is shown on the leading diagonal. A row of zeros shows an isolated vertex.
Reading a graph from a matrix: for each non-zero entry above the leading diagonal, draw that many edges between the two vertices.
check: In an adjacency matrix, what does a 2 in row B, column C mean?
There are two edges joining B and C.

p: Edges and weights: AB 4, AC 2, BC 1, BD 5, CD 8, CE 10, DE 2. Start at A. The cheapest edge from A is AC (2). From {A, C}, the cheapest edge to a new vertex is CB (1). From {A, B, C}, the options to new vertices are BD (5), CD (8) and CE (10): choose BD (5). From {A, B, C, D}, the cheapest edge to E is DE (2).

The minimum spanning tree is AC, CB, BD, DE, with total weight 2 + 1 + 5 + 2 = 10. It has 4 edges for 5 vertices, as every spanning tree must. AB was never chosen because it would join two vertices already connected, creating a cycle.
check: How many edges does a spanning tree of a connected graph with 8 vertices have?

fig.cap: Prim’s algorithm from A picks AC (2), CB (1), BD (5), DE (2): a minimum spanning tree of weight 10 (highlighted).

notes.h: Worked example: a shortest path by inspection
p: In the same network, find the shortest path from A to E. List candidate routes: A–C–E = 12; A–C–D–E = 12; A–B–D–E = 11; A–C–B–D–E = 2 + 1 + 5 + 2 = 10. The shortest path is A–C–B–D–E, length 10.
For larger networks, list systematically or use Dijkstra’s algorithm (Units 3 and 4). Note that the shortest path need not visit every vertex; here it happens to.
Forgetting the outside face. Counting a loop as degree 1. Mixing up Eulerian and Hamiltonian. Giving a shortest path when a minimum spanning tree is asked for, or the reverse.

topics.title: Linear relations and measurement
points: Linear model: \(y = a + bx\), where \(a\) is the intercept and \(b\) the gradient (rate of change).
Simultaneous equations: solve by substitution, elimination or graphing. Break-even is where cost \(=\) revenue.
Pythagoras: \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\). Right triangles: \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{O}{H}\), \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{A}{H}\), \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{O}{A}\).
Sine rule \(\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}\); cosine rule \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C\).
Similar figures with scale factor \(k\): lengths \(\times k\), areas \(\times k^2\), volumes \(\times k^3\).
Circle \(A = \pi r^2\); cylinder \(V = \pi r^2 h\); sphere \(V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\).
topics.explain: Explain why doubling every length of a box multiplies its volume by \(8\).

A business has fixed costs of $[[=(p-c)*m|,0]]. Each item costs $[[c]] to make and sells for $[[p]]. How many items must it sell to break even?

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with substituting into formulas and solving linear equations.

The big idea: many everyday situations follow straight-line rules (costs, charges, conversions), and many practical problems involve lengths, angles, areas and volumes. This lesson brings together linear modelling and measurement, both of which reward careful setting out and correct units.

A linear model has a constant rate of change. In \(y = a + bx\), the intercept \(a\) is the starting value and the slope \(b\) is the rate. Example: a plumber charges an $80 call-out fee plus $60 per hour: \(C = 80 + 60t\). A 2.5-hour job costs \(80 + 150 = \$230\). Models only apply over the range for which they make sense.

Example: a stall has fixed costs of $120 and each item costs $4 to make and sells for $10. Cost \(C = 120 + 4n\); revenue \(R = 10n\). Break-even when \(10n = 120 + 4n\), so \(n = 20\) items. Selling more than 20 makes a profit.
Elimination example: \(2x + 3y = 13\) and \(x - 3y = -1\). Adding gives \(3x = 12\), so \(x = 4\) and \(y = \tfrac{5}{3}\).

fig.cap: Cost C = 120 + 4n and revenue R = 10n meet at the break-even point (20, 200). Beyond 20 items the stall makes a profit.

p: A piecewise linear graph uses different lines over different intervals, such as a taxi fare with a higher rate after a certain distance. A step graph is constant over each interval and jumps between them, such as parking fees. An open circle means the endpoint is not included; a closed circle means it is.

Right-angled: use Pythagoras for sides and SOH CAH TOA for a side and an angle. Non-right-angled: use the sine rule when you know a side and its opposite angle; use the cosine rule when you know two sides and the included angle, or three sides. Area \(= \tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C\).

Example: two sides of 8 m and 11 m enclose an angle of 50°. Third side: \(c^2 = 64 + 121 - 176\cos 50^\circ = 71.87\), so \(c = 8.48\) m. Area \(= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 11 \times \sin 50^\circ = 33.7\) m².

Similar shapes have equal angles and sides in the same ratio \(k\). Example: a model is built at a scale of 1 : 20. Lengths are multiplied by 20, areas by \(20^2 = 400\) and volumes by \(20^3 = 8000\). A model tank holding 0.5 L corresponds to a real tank of 4000 L.
check: Two similar cylinders have a length scale factor of 3. How do their volumes compare?
The larger volume is 27 times the smaller.

p: Convert before calculating. For area units square the conversion factor (1 m² = 10 000 cm²); for volume cube it (1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1 m³ = 1000 L). Round only at the end, to the accuracy the question asks for.

notes.h: Worked example: a line from two points
p: A taxi charges $13 for a 2 km trip and $29 for a 6 km trip. Slope \(= \dfrac{29 - 13}{6 - 2} = 4\) dollars per km. Intercept: \(13 = a + 4 \times 2\), so \(a = 5\). Model: \(C = 5 + 4d\).
Interpretation: the flag fall is $5 and each kilometre costs $4. A 10 km trip would cost $45.
check: A plumber charges $150 for 1 hour and $270 for 3 hours. Find the linear model.

notes.h: Worked example: bearings and the cosine rule
p: A boat sails 8 km on a bearing of 040°, then 5 km on a bearing of 100°. At the turning point the angle between the two legs is 180° − (100° − 40°) = 120°.

Distance from the start: \(d^2 = 8^2 + 5^2 - 2 \times 8 \times 5 \times \cos 120^\circ = 89 + 40 = 129\), so \(d \approx 11.36\) km. Always draw a diagram with north lines at each point; most errors in bearing questions come from the angle at the turn.

p: Break a shape into parts you know. A water tank is a cylinder of radius 1 m and height 3 m with a hemispherical top. Volume \(= \pi(1)^2(3) + \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{4}{3}\pi(1)^3 = 3\pi + \tfrac{2}{3}\pi \approx 11.52\ \mathrm{m^3}\), which is about 11 520 litres.
For surface area, add only the faces that are exposed; the circle where the hemisphere joins the cylinder is inside the tank and is not counted.
Calculator in radian mode. Using the sine rule when the cosine rule is needed. Scaling an area by \(k\) instead of \(k^2\). Forgetting the bearing is measured clockwise from north.

topics.title: Variation and non-linear relations
points: Direct variation: \(y = kx\); the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Inverse variation: \(y = \dfrac{k}{x}\); as \(x\) doubles, \(y\) halves.
Variation with powers: \(y = kx^2\), \(y = kx^3\), \(y = \dfrac{k}{x^2}\).
Find \(k\) from one known pair of values, then use the rule.
Plotting \(y\) against a transformed \(x\) (such as \(x^2\) or \(\dfrac{1}{x}\)) gives a straight line through the origin when the variation model fits.
topics.explain: Explain why the time a trip takes varies inversely with average speed, using a 120 km trip as your example.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with linear models and with substituting into formulas.

The big idea: not every relationship is a straight line. Many follow a simple rule in which one variable is proportional to another, to its square, or to its reciprocal. Recognising which rule fits, and finding its constant, lets you make predictions from just one pair of measurements.
\(y\) varies directly as \(x\) if \(y = kx\) for some constant \(k\), the constant of variation. Doubling \(x\) doubles \(y\). The graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient \(k\).
Example: the cost of fuel varies directly with the number of litres. 40 L cost $76, so \(k = \dfrac{76}{40} = 1.9\) dollars per litre, and 55 L cost \(1.9 \times 55 = \$104.50\).
check: \(y\) varies directly as \(x\), and \(y = 12\) when \(x = 3\). Find \(y\) when \(x = 10\).

p: \(y\) varies inversely as \(x\) if \(y = \dfrac{k}{x}\). Doubling \(x\) halves \(y\), and the product \(xy\) is constant. The graph is a hyperbola that approaches both axes without touching them.
Example: the time for a 120 km trip is \(t = \dfrac{120}{v}\). At 60 km/h it takes 2 hours; at 80 km/h, 1.5 hours; at 120 km/h, 1 hour.
check: \(y\) varies inversely as \(x\), and \(y = 6\) when \(x = 4\). Find \(y\) when \(x = 8\).

fig.cap: Direct variation y = 2x is a straight line through the origin; inverse variation y = 12/x is a hyperbola where doubling x halves y.

p: The stopping distance of a car varies roughly as the square of its speed: \(d = kv^2\). If \(d = 20\) m at 50 km/h, then \(k = \dfrac{20}{2500} = 0.008\), and at 100 km/h \(d = 0.008 \times 10\,000 = 80\) m. Doubling the speed multiplies the distance by four.

The volume of similar containers varies as the cube of a length: \(V = kl^3\). The intensity of light varies inversely as the square of the distance from the source: \(I = \dfrac{k}{d^2}\), so doubling the distance gives a quarter of the intensity.

To check whether data follow \(y = kx^2\), make a new column of \(x^2\) values and plot \(y\) against \(x^2\). If the points lie close to a straight line through the origin, the model fits, and its gradient is \(k\). The same method tests \(y = \dfrac{k}{x}\) by plotting \(y\) against \(\dfrac{1}{x}\).
This idea, straightening a curve by transforming a variable, returns in Units 3 and 4 as data transformation in regression.

Assuming any relationship that increases is direct variation. Forgetting that inverse variation means the product is constant, not the difference. Squaring the wrong quantity when finding \(k\). Using a linear model with a non-zero intercept when the question says “varies directly”, which requires the line to pass through the origin.
